newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. businessmen slam calls for sanctions on Burma.
newsitem.headline: U.S. businessmen slam calls for sanctions on Burma.

text.p: Top American businessmen said on Monday that economic sanctions would fail to move Burma towards democracy and reforms were more likely to come from "constructive engagement".
Speaking during a one-day meeting of the U.S./ASEAN Business Council, they said unilateral sanctions were particularly undesirable.
Former U.S. secretary of state Alexander Haig told a news conference the United States achieved more by dialogue and communication than by finger-wagging, criticism or blackmail.

"Every analysis I have seen suggests that not only do sanctions not work, but they frequently, especially in democratic societies, create obstacles for the incumbent leaders of those societies to make the changes we want," he said.
"It is a very short-sighted approach," he added.
"It's arrogant, it's wrong-headed and it misreads the lessons of history," said Haig, president of consultants Worldwide Associates Inc.

He and some 50 other leaders of top U.S. firms were meeting their counterparts from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
ASEAN, which is ready to admit Burma as a member, probably later this year, opposes sanctions on the military-led government in Rangoon.
It says "constructive engagement" -- maintaining normal ties while pushing for change -- is the correct approach.
Former U.S. treasury secretary Lloyd Bentsen said unilateral economic sanctions did not accomplish their objectives.
"I think a constructive engagement is much more important for the U.S.. We shouldn't lose what little influence we do have by pulling out. You can't get it by just walking away," he said.
Bentsen called Burmese democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who has repeatedly called for sanctions on Rangoon, a remarkable person, but he did not agree with her.
"I sympathise with her problem. However, we are a nation and we can't govern by the ideas and the recommendations of one person. I don't agree with her," he said.
"We have to look to see what we can do to liberalise the situation in Burma and protect people like her," he added.
